is the propensity score we’d estimate with knowledge of $\eta$ , i.e., by taking $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ . Conclude by the previous step that $\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n})$ , and show the same convergence rate holds for $\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}$ by empirical process arguments.

### Step 1

Strong concavity will be proven using calculus along with Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2. First, we notice that by Assumption 5.2(c) and (74), we know $\nabla\Psi(A)|_{A=M(e^{*})}\succcurlyeq m^{*}I$ for some $m^{*}>0$ . Then by continuity of the smallest eigenvalue function $\lambda_{\min}(\cdot)$ and of $\nabla\Psi(\cdot)$ , there exists $r_{0}>0$ such that if $e\in\mathcal{E}$ satisfies $\|e-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\leqslant r_{0}$ (which implies $\|M(e)-M(e^{*})\|\leqslant Cr_{0}$ by (72)), then $M(e)\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/2)I$ and $\nabla\Psi(A)|_{A=M(e)}\succcurlyeq(m^{*}/2)I$ . We now extend this argument to provide a high probability eigenvalue lower bound on $\hat{M}_{n}(e)$ for $e$ sufficiently close to $\hat{e}$ in $L^{2}(\mathcal{X},P_{n})$ :

#### Lemma C.1.

Suppose that all conditions of Lemma 5.2 hold. Fix any $k_{0}>0$ and define $A_{n}$ to be the event that $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ . Then there exist $\tilde{r}>0$ and $0<\tilde{k}<\tilde{K}$ such that whenever $A_{n}$ holds, for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\|e-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}$ we have $\hat{M}_{n}(e)\succcurlyeq(k_{0}/2)I$ and $\tilde{K}I\succcurlyeq\nabla\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e))\succcurlyeq\tilde{k}I$ .

#### Proof of Lemma C.1.

The function $\lambda_{\min}(\cdot)$ is uniformly continuous on the compact subset $\mathcal{M}=\{A:0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq CI\}$ of p×p. Hence, when the event $A_{n}$ holds, we know that there exists (nonrandom) $\tilde{\delta}>0$ such that $A\succcurlyeq(k_{0}/2)I$ for all $A\in\mathcal{M}$ with $\|A-\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\|\leqslant\tilde{\delta}$ . By (73), $\mathcal{M}$ contains both $\{M(e):e\in\mathcal{E}\}$ and $\{\hat{M}_{n}(e):e\in\mathcal{E}\}$ . Noting that

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{M}_{n}(e_{1})-\hat{M}_{n}(e_{2})\| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|f(e_{1}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e_{2}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i})\| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|e_{1}(X_{i})-e_{2}(X_{i})| \displaystyle\leqslant C\|e_{1}-e_{2}\|_{2,P_{n}}. $$

we see that whenever $e\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\|e-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}:=\tilde{\delta}/C$ , we have $\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\|\leqslant\tilde{\delta}$ and hence $\hat{M}_{n}(e)\succcurlyeq(k_{0}/2)I$ . The conclusion of Lemma C.1 follows immediately by Assumption 5.2(c). ∎

Next, we bound directional derivatives of $\phi$ and $\hat{\phi}_{n}$ .

#### Lemma C.2.

For any $e_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}$ with $M(e_{1})$ and $M(e_{2})$ nonsingular, the inequality

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\phi(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1}))\leqslant\textnormal{tr}\left[\nabla\Psi(M(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1})))^{\top}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}M(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1}))\right)\right] $$

holds for each $t\in(0,1)$ . Similarly, for any $e_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ with $\hat{M}_{n}(e_{1})$ and $\hat{M}_{n}(e_{2})$ nonsingular, we have the inequality

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1}))\leqslant\textnormal{tr}\biggl[\nabla\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1})))^{\top}\biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\hat{M}_{n}(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1}))\biggr)\biggr]. $$

#### Proof of Lemma C.2.

Fix $e_{1}=e_{1}(\cdot)$ and $e_{2}=e_{2}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}$ with $M(e_{1})$ and $M(e_{2})$ invertible. Define

$$ \tilde{M}(t)=M(e_{(t)}) $$

where $e_{(t)}=e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1})$ . We first show that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(x),\eta(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x),\quad\forall t\in[0,1],\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))^{2}f^{\prime\prime}(e_{(t)}(x),\eta(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x),\quad\forall t\in(0,1). $$

We include the endpoints $t=0,1$ in (81) so that we can apply Taylor’s theorem with the Lagrange form of the second order remainder to complete the proof of Lemma C.2. We could also strengthen (82) to include those endpoints, but this will not be needed.

Consider the difference quotient

$$ D_{1}(t,h;X)=\frac{f(e_{(t+h)}(X),\eta(X))-f(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X))}{h} $$

By the chain rule we know that

$$ \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}D_{1}(t,h;X)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X))=(e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X))f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X)). $$

Furthermore the fact that $e_{1}(x),e_{2}(x)\in[0,1]$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ indicates

$$ \tilde{\delta}\leqslant-h\leqslant e_{(t)}(x)\wedge e_{(t+h)}(x)\leqslant e_{(t)}(x)\vee e_{(t+h)}(x)\leqslant 1+h\leqslant 1-\tilde{\delta} $$

for all $t\in[0,1]$ and $|h|\leqslant-\tilde{\delta}$ . By uniform boundedness of $f^{\prime}$ on $[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]\times\mathcal{W}$ and Taylor’s theorem, and noting $e_{(t+h)}(x)-e_{(t)}(x)=h(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))$ we conclude that

$$ \sup_{0<|h|\leqslant-\tilde{\delta}}\|D_{1}(t,h;X)\|\leqslant|e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X)|\times\sup_{e\in[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]}\|f^{\prime}(e,\eta(X))\|\leqslant C $$

so by dominated convergence

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tilde{M}(t+h)-\tilde{M}(t)}{h} \displaystyle=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\int_{\mathcal{X}}D_{1}(t,h;x)\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(x),\eta(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x) $$

which establishes (81).

Similarly we define the second difference quotient

$$ D_{2}(t,h;X)=\frac{f^{\prime}(e_{(t+h)}(X),\eta(X))-f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X))}{h}. $$

By the chain rule we once again have

$$ \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}D_{2}(t,h;X)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X))=(e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X))f^{\prime\prime}(e_{(t)}(X),\eta(X)). $$

By uniform boundedness of $f^{\prime\prime}$ on $[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]\times\mathcal{W}$ we get

$$ \sup_{0<|h|\leqslant-\tilde{\delta}}|D_{2}(t,h;X)|\leqslant|e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X)|\times\sup_{e\in[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]}\|f^{\prime\prime}(e,\eta(X))\|\leqslant C. $$

Then in view of (81) we can apply dominated convergence to conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t+h)-\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t)}{h} \displaystyle=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\int_{\mathcal{X}}D_{2}(t,h;x)(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(e_{2}(x)-e_{1}(x))^{2}f^{\prime\prime}(e_{(t)}(x),\eta(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x) $$

establishing (82).

Now we differentiate $\tilde{\phi}(t):=\phi(e_{(t)})$ . Note $M(e_{(t)})\succ 0$ for all $t\in[0,1]$ by concavity of $M(\cdot)$ , shown previously. Then using (81) and (82), we apply the chain rule to get

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\prime}(t) \displaystyle=\textnormal{tr}\bigl[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t)\bigr],\quad t\in[0,1]. $$

Similarly for all $t\in(0,1)$

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\prime\prime}(t) \displaystyle=D^{2}\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))(\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t),\tilde{M}^{\prime}(t))+\textnormal{tr}[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)] \displaystyle\leqslant\textnormal{tr}\bigl[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)\bigr], $$

which shows (79). Here $D^{2}\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))$ is the second derivative mapping of $\Psi$ evaluated at $\tilde{M}(t)$ , viewed as a bilinear function from $\real{}^{p\times p}\times\real^{p\times p}$ to ; the inequality in the preceding display follows from concavity of $\Psi$ .

Equation (80) follows by a very similar calculation, though the argument is simplified, since dominated convergence is no longer needed as we are dealing with finite sums instead of integrals. Instead we immediately perform term-by-term differentiation to conclude

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime}(t) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(e_{2}(X_{i})-e_{1}(X_{i}))f^{\prime}(e_{(t)}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i})),\quad\forall t\in[0,1],\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(e_{2}(X_{i})-e_{1}(X_{i}))^{2}f^{\prime\prime}(e_{(t)}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i})),\quad\forall t\in(0,1) $$

where $\tilde{M}_{n}(t):=\hat{M}_{n}(e_{(t)})$ , and then use the chain rule as above. ∎

We are now ready to prove (75). We apply Lemma C.2 with $e_{1}=e^{*}$ and any $e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\|e_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\leqslant r_{0}$ . Note that our definition of $r_{0}$ (in the paragraph before the statement of Lemma C.1) along with (74) ensures that $M(e_{1})$ and $M(e_{2})$ are nonsingular. Also, note that $\tilde{\phi}^{\prime}(0)\leqslant 0$ by optimality of $e^{*}$ . Lemma C.2 along with Taylor’s theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder then enables us to conclude

$$ \phi(e_{2})=\tilde{\phi}(1)=\tilde{\phi}(0)+\tilde{\phi}^{\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\phi}^{\prime\prime}(t)\leqslant\phi(e^{*})+\frac{1}{2}\textnormal{tr}\bigl[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)\bigr] $$

for some $t\in(0,1)$ , where $\tilde{M}(t)=M(e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1}))$ as in the proof of Lemma C.2. By (29) and (82), we know that $\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)\preccurlyeq 0$ . Recalling that the trace of the product of two symmetric positive semidefinite matrices is nonnegative, we have

$$ 0\geqslant\textnormal{tr}[(\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))-(m^{*}/2)I)^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)]=\textnormal{tr}[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)]-\frac{m^{*}}{2}\textnormal{tr}(\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)) $$

since $\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))\succcurlyeq(m^{*}/2)I$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\textnormal{tr}[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)] \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{m^{*}}{2}\textnormal{tr}(\tilde{M}^{\prime\prime}(t)) \displaystyle\leqslant-\frac{cm^{*}}{2}\int_{\mathcal{X}}(e^{*}(x)-e_{2}(x))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle=-\frac{cm^{*}}{2}\|e^{*}-e_{2}\|_{2,P}^{2} $$

where the second inequality follows by (29) and (82) once again. We conclude that whenever $e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\|e_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\leqslant r_{0}$ we have

$$ \phi(e^{*})\geqslant\phi(e_{2})+\frac{cm^{*}}{4}\|e_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}^{2}. $$

Now take any $e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}$ with $\|e_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}>r_{0}$ . Define $t=1-r_{0}/\|e_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\in(0,1)$ and consider $\tilde{e}_{2}=te^{*}+(1-t)e_{2}$ so that $\|\tilde{e}_{2}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}=r_{0}$ . Note $\tilde{e}_{2}\in\mathcal{F}$ by convexity of $\mathcal{F}_{*}$ , so by the preceding display

$$ \phi(e^{*})\geqslant\phi(\tilde{e}_{2})+\frac{cm^{*}r_{0}^{2}}{4}\geqslant t\phi(e^{*})+(1-t)\phi(e_{2})+\frac{cm^{*}r_{0}^{2}}{4} $$

where the second inequality is by concavity of $\phi$ . Rearranging we have

$$ \phi(e^{*})\geqslant\phi(e_{2})+\frac{cm^{*}r_{0}^{2}}{4(1-t)}=\phi(e_{2})+\frac{cm^{*}r_{0}}{4}\|e^{*}-e_{2}\|_{2,P}. $$

Letting $c_{0}=cm^{*}/4$ , we conclude that for all $e\in\mathcal{F}$ we have

$$ \phi(e^{*})\geqslant\phi(e)+c_{0}\min(r_{0},\|e^{*}-e\|_{2,P})\|e^{*}-e\|_{2,P} $$

which shows (75).

The proof of (76) is quite similar. Take $k_{0}>0$ such that with $k^{*}$ as in (74), whenever $0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq CI$ with $\Psi(A)\geqslant\inf_{B\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/4)I}\Psi(B)$ , we have $A\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ . Such a $k_{0}$ exists by Assumptions 5.2(a) and 5.2(d). By Lemma C.1, on the truncation event $A_{n}$ that $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ , we have $\tilde{K}I\geqslant\nabla\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e))\geqslant\tilde{k}I$ whenever $\|e-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}$ , for some $\tilde{r}>0$ and $0<\tilde{k}<\tilde{K}$ . Now we apply (80) with $e_{1}=\hat{e}$ and any $e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ with $\|e_{2}-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}$ (note we must have $\hat{M}_{n}(e_{1})$ and $\hat{M}_{n}(e_{2})$ nonsingular). Defining $\tilde{\phi}_{n}(t):=\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{(t)})$ for $e_{(t)}=e_{1}+t(e_{2}-e_{1})$ , by optimality of $\hat{e}$ we must have $\tilde{\phi}_{n}^{\prime}(0)\leqslant 0$ . Taylor’s theorem and the second part of Lemma C.2 then allow us to conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{2})\bm{1}(A_{n})=\tilde{\phi}_{n}(1)\bm{1}(A_{n}) \displaystyle=\Bigl(\tilde{\phi}_{n}(0)+\tilde{\phi}_{n}^{\prime}(0)+\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\phi}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)\Bigr)\bm{1}(A_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\Bigl(\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})+\frac{1}{2}\textnormal{tr}\bigl[\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}_{n}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)\bigr]\Bigr)\bm{1}(A_{n}) $$

for some $t\in(0,1)$ , where $\tilde{M}_{n}(t)=\hat{M}_{n}(e_{(t)})$ as in the proof of Lemma C.2. With $\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}_{n}(t))\succcurlyeq\tilde{k}I$ for all $t\in(0,1)$ whenever $A_{n}$ holds, we have by (84) that

$$ 0\geqslant\textnormal{tr}\bigl[(\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}_{n}(t))-\tilde{k}I)^{\top}\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)\bigr]\bm{1}(A_{n})=\bigl(\textnormal{tr}[(\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}_{n}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)]-\tilde{k}\textnormal{tr}[\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)]\bigr)\bm{1}(A_{n}). $$

Hence by (29)

$$ \textnormal{tr}[(\nabla\Psi(\tilde{M}_{n}(t))^{\top}\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)]\bm{1}(A_{n})\leqslant\tilde{k}\textnormal{tr}[\tilde{M}_{n}^{\prime\prime}(t)]\bm{1}(A_{n})\leqslant-\tilde{k}c\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}\bm{1}(A_{n}). $$

Then by (85) we conclude that whenever $\|e-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}$ we have

$$ (\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e))\bm{1}(A_{n})\geqslant c\frac{\tilde{k}}{2}\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}\bm{1}(A_{n}). $$

Redefining $r_{0}$ to be the minimum of the $r_{0}$ appearing in the proof of (75) and $\tilde{r}$ , since $\hat{\phi}_{n}$ is always concave on $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ . we can repeat the argument at the end of the proof of (75) to conclude that

$$ (\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e))\bm{1}(A_{n})\geqslant\left(c_{0}\min(r_{0},\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}})\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}}\right)\bm{1}(A_{n}) $$

for all $e\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ ; here $c_{0}:=c\tilde{k}/2>0$ .

### Step 2

Fix $\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\in\mathcal{F}_{*}$ and $e_{n}^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ . The result of Step 1 shows that for some positive constants $c_{0}$ and $r_{0}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle c_{0}\min(r_{0},\|e^{*}-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\|_{2,P})\|e^{*}-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\|_{2,P} \displaystyle\leqslant\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle c_{0}\min(r_{0},\|\hat{e}-e_{n}^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}})\|\hat{e}-e_{n}^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}\bm{1}(A_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant(\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}))\bm{1}(A_{n}). $$

With $\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\geqslant 0$ and $\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})\geqslant 0$ by the definitions of $e^{*}$ and $\hat{e}$ , we can further upper bound the right-hand sides by

$$ \displaystyle\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}) \displaystyle\leqslant\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})+\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle(\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}))\bm{1}(A_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})+\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}). $$

### Step 3

For brevity, in this section we introduce the empirical process notation

$$ Pe=\int_{\mathcal{X}}e(x)\,\mathrm{d}P(x) $$

for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ . For instance, with $P_{n}$ the empirical measure induced by $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ , we have $P_{n}e=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}$ for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ .

We first show that we can choose particular $\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}=\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}$ and $e_{n}^{*}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ that are very close in sup norm to $\hat{e}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ and $e^{*}\in\mathcal{F}$ , respectively, with high probability.

#### Lemma C.3.

Under the conditions of Lemma 5.2, there exist $\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}=\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}$ and $e_{n}^{*}=e_{n}^{*}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ such that $\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|\hat{e}(x)-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}(x)|+\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|e^{*}(x)-e_{n}^{*}(x)|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ .

#### Proof of Lemma C.3.

With the functions in $\mathcal{E}$ uniformly bounded by 1, by Lemma B.3 we conclude

$$ \mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\Big|P_{n}e-Pe\Big|\right]\leqslant KCn^{-1/2} $$

so that $\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big|P_{n}e-Pe\big|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ by Markov’s inequality. In view of the fact that $m_{L}\leqslant P_{n}\hat{e}\leqslant m_{H}$ and $m_{L}\leqslant Pe^{*}\leqslant m_{H}$ since $\hat{e}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ and $e^{*}\in\mathcal{F}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle m_{L}-\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big|P_{n}e-Pe\big| \displaystyle\leqslant P_{n}e^{*}\leqslant m_{H}+\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big|P_{n}e-Pe\big|,\quad\text{and} \displaystyle m_{L}-\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big|P_{n}e-Pe\big| \displaystyle\leqslant P\hat{e}\leqslant m_{H}+\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\big|P_{n}e-Pe\big|. $$

Next, with $e_{L}=e_{L}(\cdot)$ and $e_{H}=e_{H}(\cdot)$ as in the assumptions of Lemma 5.2, define

$$ e_{n}^{*}(x)=\begin{cases}e^{*}(x),&m_{L}\leqslant P_{n}e^{*}\leqslant m_{H}\\
e^{*}(x)+\lambda_{n}(e_{L}(x)-e^{*}(x)),&P_{n}e^{*}<m_{L}\\
e^{*}(x)+\lambda_{n}(e_{H}(x)-e^{*}(x)),&P_{n}e^{*}>m_{H}\end{cases} $$

where

$$ \lambda_{n}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{m_{L}-P_{n}e^{*}}{P_{n}[e_{L}-e^{*}]},&P_{n}e^{*}<m_{L}\\[8.61108pt]
\dfrac{P_{n}e^{*}-m_{H}}{P_{n}[e^{*}-e_{H}]},&P_{n}e^{*}>m_{H}\\[8.61108pt]
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

On the event

$$ A_{n}=\left\{P_{n}e_{L}\geqslant\frac{Pe_{L}+m_{L}}{2},P_{n}e_{H}\leqslant\frac{Pe_{H}+m_{H}}{2}\right\} $$

we must have $0\leqslant\lambda_{n}\leqslant 1$ since $Pe_{L}>m_{L}$ and $Pe_{H}<m_{H}$ , and so when $A_{n}$ holds we know $e_{n}^{*}\in\mathcal{E}$ by convexity of $\mathcal{E}$ . Furthermore we have $P_{n}e_{n}^{*}=\max(m_{L},\min(m_{H},\mathbb{E}_{P_{n}}[e^{*}(X)]))$ so that in fact $e_{n}^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ . But with $M=2\max\left((Pe_{L}-m_{L})^{-1},(m_{H}-Pe_{H})^{-1}\right)$ we have

$$ \displaystyle 0\leqslant\lambda_{n}\bm{1}(A_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant M\bm{1}(A_{n})[(m_{L}-P_{n}e^{*})\bm{1}(P_{n}e^{*}<m_{L})+(P_{n}e^{*}-m_{H})\bm{1}(P_{n}e^{*}>m_{H})] \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eq:P_n_e_star}}}{{\leqslant}}2M\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}|P_{n}e-P_{e}|\bm{1}(A_{n}). $$

With $\textnormal{Pr}(A_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ by the law of large numbers, we get $\lambda_{n}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ , and hence for each $x\in\mathcal{X}$ we have

$$ |e_{n}^{*}(x)-e^{*}(x)|\leqslant\lambda_{n}(|e_{L}(x)-e^{*}(x)|\vee|e_{H}(x)-e^{*}(x)|)\leqslant\lambda_{n}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}). $$

Next, define

$$ \hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}(x)=\begin{cases}\hat{e}(x),&m_{L}\leqslant P\hat{e}\leqslant m_{H}\\
\hat{e}(x)+\tilde{\lambda}_{n}(e_{L}(x)-\hat{e}(x)),&P\hat{e}<m_{L}\\
\hat{e}(x)+\tilde{\lambda}_{n}(e_{H}(x)-\hat{e}(x)),&P\hat{e}>m_{H}\end{cases} $$

with

$$ \tilde{\lambda}_{n}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{m_{L}-P\hat{e}}{m_{H}-\hat{e}},&P\hat{e}<m_{L}\\[8.61108pt]
\dfrac{P\hat{e}-m_{H}}{P\hat{e}-m_{L}},&P\hat{e}>m_{H}\\[8.61108pt]
0,&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases} $$

so that $0\leqslant\tilde{\lambda}_{n}\leqslant 1$ and $\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\in\mathcal{F}$ always. In fact

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\lambda}_{n} \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{M}{2}\bigl[(m_{L}-P\hat{e})\bm{1}(P\hat{e}<m_{L})+(P\hat{e}-m_{H})\bm{1}(P\hat{e}>m_{H})\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant M\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}|P_{n}e-Pe| $$

so that $\tilde{\lambda}_{n}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ as well and the lemma follows since for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$

$$ |\hat{e}(x)-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}(x)|\leqslant\tilde{\lambda}_{n}(|e_{L}(x)-\hat{e}(x)|\vee|e_{H}(x)-\hat{e}(x)|)\leqslant\tilde{\lambda}_{n}. $$

∎

We are now ready to prove consistency. Taking $\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}$ as in Lemma C.3, we upper bound the right-hand side of the inequalities in step 2:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})+\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})&\leqslant|\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e_{n}^{*})|+|\phi(e_{n}^{*})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})|\\
&\phantom{=}\ +|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|+|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|.\end{split} $$

In view of (72) and (78), Lemma C.3 shows that

$$ \displaystyle\|M(e^{*})-M(e_{n}^{*})\| \displaystyle=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\|\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\| \displaystyle=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}). $$

We now use (89) to show that

$$ |\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e_{n}^{*})|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}). $$

As shown at the start of step 1, whenever $\|e_{n}^{*}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\leqslant r_{0}$ we have $M(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/2)I$ , so that

$$ tM(e^{*})+(1-t)M(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/2)I\quad\forall t\in[0,1]. $$

Applying Taylor’s theorem to $\Psi(\cdot)$ we have for some $K<\infty$ that

$$ \displaystyle|\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e_{n}^{*})|\bm{1}(\tilde{A}_{n}) \displaystyle=|\Psi(M(e^{*}))-\Psi(M(e_{n}^{*}))|\bm{1}(\tilde{A}_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\Big|\textnormal{tr}[\nabla\Psi(tM(e^{*})+(1-t)M(e_{n}^{*}))]^{\top}[M(e^{*})-M(e_{n}^{*})])\Big|\bm{1}(\tilde{A}_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|\nabla\Psi(tM(e^{*})+(1-t)M(e_{n}^{*}))\|\cdot\|M(e^{*})-M(e_{n}^{*})\|\bm{1}(\tilde{A}_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant K\sqrt{p}\cdot\|M(e^{*})-M(e_{n}^{*})\|\bm{1}(\tilde{A}_{n}) $$

where $\tilde{A}_{n}$ is the event $\|e_{n}^{*}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\leqslant r_{0}$ and the last inequality follows from Assumption 5.2(c) and the fact that $\|A\|\leqslant\sqrt{p}\lambda_{\max}(A)$ for any $A\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{p}$ . Here $\lambda_{\max}(A)$ denotes the largest eigenvalue of $A$ . Hence $|\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e_{n}^{*})|\bm{1}(A_{n})=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ by (89). But $\textnormal{Pr}(\tilde{A}_{n})\rightarrow 1$ by (89), so indeed $|\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e_{n}^{*})|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ .

Convergence of the remaining three terms in (88) depends on the following result:

$$ \sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M(e)\|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}). $$

To show this, define

$$ M_{n}(e)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i})) $$

which replaces the estimated nuisance function $\hat{\eta}$ in the definition of $\hat{M}_{n}$ with the true $\eta$ . First note that by uniform boundedness of $\|f_{w}\|_{2}$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{e\in[0,1]}\|f(e,\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e,\eta(X_{i}))\|\leqslant Cn^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}\leqslant C\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}. $$

Then by (34) we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)\| \displaystyle=\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\bigg\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(e(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))\bigg\| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sup_{e\in[0,1]}\|f(e,\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e,\eta(X_{i}))\| \displaystyle=O_{p}(\alpha_{n}). $$

Now for $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ define the class of functions

$$ \mathcal{G}_{ij}=\{x\mapsto f_{ij}(e(x),\eta(x))\mid e\in\mathcal{E}\} $$

where $f_{ij}$ denotes the $(i,j)$ -th entry of the function $f$ . By Lemma B.4

$$ \displaystyle n^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(r,\mathcal{G}_{ij},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}r \displaystyle=Cn^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{C^{-1}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(C\epsilon,\mathcal{G}_{ij},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon \displaystyle\leqslant Cn^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{C^{-1}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{E},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon. $$

Let

$$ D(e)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))-\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(e(x),\eta(x))\,\mathrm{d}P(x)=M_{n}(e)-M(e). $$

Then Lemma B.3 and Assumption 5.1 indicate that $\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}|D_{ij}(e)|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ and so

$$ \sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|D(e)\|=\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\biggl(\,\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p}D_{ij}(e)^{2}\biggr)^{1/2}\leqslant\biggl(\,\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}|D_{ij}(e)|^{2}\biggr)^{1/2}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}). $$

The result (93) follows by the triangle inequality in view of (94) and (95).

We are finally ready to bound the remaining terms on the right-hand side of (88), and show that $\textnormal{Pr}(A_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ where $A_{n}$ is the event $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ for $k_{0}>0$ defined in Step 1. Choose $\delta>0$ so that for any $A_{1}$ , $A_{2}$ in $\mathcal{M}=\{A\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{p}:0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq CI\}$ , with $\|A_{1}-A_{2}\|\leqslant\delta$ , we have $|\lambda_{\min}(A_{1})-\lambda_{\min}(A_{2})|\leqslant\min(k_{0}/2,k^{*}/4)$ , where $k^{*}$ satisfies (74). Such $\delta$ exists by uniform continuity of $\lambda_{\min}(\cdot)$ on the compact subset $\mathcal{M}$ of p×p (cf. the proof of Lemma C.1). Also define the event $B_{n}$ that all of the following are true:

$$ \displaystyle\|e_{n}^{*}-e^{*}\|_{2,P} \displaystyle\leqslant r_{0}, \displaystyle\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M(e)\| \displaystyle\leqslant\delta\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\|\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\| \displaystyle\leqslant\delta. $$

We claim that $B_{n}$ implies the following conditions:

$$ M(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq\frac{k^{*}}{2}I,\quad\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq\frac{k^{*}}{4}I,\quad\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I\quad\text{and}\quad\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\succcurlyeq\frac{k_{0}}{2}I. $$

We prove these statements briefly. Assume $B_{n}$ holds. First, note that $M(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/2)I$ holds by definition of $r_{0}$ and (96). Next, the definition of $\delta$ immediately ensures by (97) that $\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/4)I$ . But then

$$ \Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}))\geqslant\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}))\geqslant\inf_{B\succcurlyeq(k^{*}/4)I}\Psi(B) $$

so that $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ by the definition of $k_{0}$ , and in particular we have shown $B_{n}\subseteq A_{n}$ . Finally (98) shows $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\succcurlyeq(k_{0}/2)I$ .

Now take $\tilde{K}<\infty$ to be as derived from Assumption 5.2(c) with $k=\min(k^{*}/4,k_{0}/2)$ and $K=C$ . Then repeated applications of arguments analogous to (92) show that

$$ \displaystyle|\phi(e_{n}^{*})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle=|\Psi(M(e_{n}^{*}))-\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*}))|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq\tilde{K}I}|\textnormal{tr}(A^{\top}[M(e_{n}^{*})-\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})])| \displaystyle\leqslant\tilde{K}\sqrt{p}\cdot\|M(e_{n}^{*})-\hat{M}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})\| \displaystyle=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}) $$

by (93) and similarly

$$ \displaystyle|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|\bm{1}(B_{n})\leqslant\tilde{K}\sqrt{p}\cdot\|\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) $$

by (90). Also

$$ \displaystyle|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|\bm{1}(B_{n})\leqslant\tilde{K}\sqrt{p}\cdot\|\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})-M(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})\|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}) $$

by (93).

However, by (89), (72), (90), and (93) we know that $\textnormal{Pr}(B_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Since $B_{n}\subseteq A_{n}$ we also have $\textnormal{Pr}(A_{n})\rightarrow 1$ . We conclude from the preceding displays that

$$ |\phi(e_{n}^{*})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})|+|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|+|\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}). $$

Then by step 2, (88), and (91), we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\|e^{*}-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\|_{2,P} \displaystyle=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}^{-1/2})\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\|\hat{e}-e_{n}^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}} \displaystyle=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}^{-1/2}). $$

But by Lemma C.3 we know that $\|\hat{e}-\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}}\|_{2,P}+\|e^{*}-e_{n}^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ . So by the triangle inequality we conclude $\|e^{*}-\hat{e}\|_{2,P}+\|e^{*}-\hat{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}^{-1/2})$ as well.

### Step 4

The final step in the argument to derive our best convergence rates is a variation of a standard “peeling” argument used in deriving convergence rates of $M$ -estimators. The main argument requires deriving a bound on the “locally centered empirical process” as in our next result.

#### Lemma C.4.

For each $e\in\mathcal{E}$ , let $\phi_{n}(e)=\Psi(M_{n}(e))$ and take $\tilde{e}\in\argmax_{e\in\mathcal{F}_{n}}\phi_{n}(e)$ . Then there exists $\beta>0$ and a universal constant $C_{0}<\infty$ such that for all $u\leqslant\beta$

$$ \sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u}\bigl[(\hat{\phi}_{n}(e)-\phi_{n}(e))-(\hat{\phi}_{n}(\tilde{e})-\phi_{n}(\tilde{e}))\bigr]\bm{1}(B_{n})\leqslant C_{0}\bigl(u\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}\bigr) $$

for some sequence of events $B_{n}$ with $\textnormal{Pr}(B_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ .

#### Proof of Lemma C.4.

Let $U_{n}(e)=\hat{\phi}_{n}(e)-\phi_{n}(e)$ for each $e\in\mathcal{E}$ . By Taylor’s theorem, for each $e\in\mathcal{E}$

$$ U_{n}(e)=\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e))-\Psi(M_{n}(e))=\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))^{\top}(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)) $$

for some $R_{n}(e)$ lying on the line segment between $M_{n}(e)$ and $\hat{M}_{n}(e)$ . Write

$$ \displaystyle U_{n}(e)-U_{n}(\tilde{e}) \displaystyle=(\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))-\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e})))^{\top}(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e}))^{\top}[(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e))-(\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-M_{n}(\tilde{e}))]. $$

Because $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ trivially satisfies the conditions of Lemma 5.2, all of our results in steps 1–3 apply if we replace $\hat{M}_{n}$ with $M_{n}$ . In particular with $k_{0}>0$ as chosen in step 1, we have $\textnormal{Pr}(M_{n}(\tilde{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I)\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ by the argument at the end of step 3. Take $\tilde{r}$ , $\tilde{k}$ , and $\tilde{K}$ derived from Lemma C.1 with this choice of $k_{0}$ . By the proof of Lemma C.1, we know that for all $0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq CI$ with $\|A-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\leqslant C\tilde{r}$ , we must have $A\succcurlyeq(k_{0}/2)I$ and $\tilde{K}I\succcurlyeq\nabla\Psi(A)\succcurlyeq\tilde{k}I$ . Let $B_{n}$ be the intersection of the events $M_{n}(\tilde{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ and $\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)\|\leqslant C\tilde{r}/3$ . Now $\textnormal{Pr}(B_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ by (94). Then for any $e\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}/3$ , in view of (78) we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})\|+\|\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{2C\tilde{r}}{3}\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\|M_{n}(e)-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\|M_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(e)\|\bm{1}(B_{n})+\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant C\tilde{r}. $$

We conclude by the preceding display that whenever $B_{n}$ holds, for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\tilde{r}/3$ we have $(k_{0}/2)I\preccurlyeq\hat{M}_{n}(e)\preccurlyeq CI$ and $(k_{0}/2)I\preccurlyeq M_{n}(e)\preccurlyeq CI$ , and thus $(k_{0}/2)I\preccurlyeq R_{n}(e)\preccurlyeq CI$ along with $\tilde{K}I\succcurlyeq\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))\succcurlyeq\tilde{k}I$ . Then by Assumption 5.2(b), for all $u\leqslant\tilde{r}/3$ there exists a constant $K_{0}<\infty$ (independent of $u$ ) for which

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))-\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e}))\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant K_{0}\|R_{n}(e)-R_{n}(\tilde{e})\|\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant K_{0}(\|R_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(e)\|+\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})\|+\|\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-R_{n}(\tilde{e})\|) $$

The preceding inequality holds for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u$ . Taking a supremum over such $e(\cdot)$ , another application of (78) and the fact that $\|R_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(e)\|\leqslant\|M_{n}(e)-\hat{M}_{n}(e)\|$ for all $e\in\mathcal{E}$ show that

$$ \sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u}\|\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))-\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e}))\|\bm{1}(B_{n})\leqslant K_{0}\bigl(Cu+2S_{n}(\mathcal{E})\bigr) $$

where $S_{n}(\mathcal{E})=\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\|\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)\|$ . Then by Cauchy-Schwarz

$$ \begin{split}\phantom{=}\ &\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u}\bigl|(\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(e))-\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e})))^{\top}(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e))\bigr|\bm{1}(B_{n})\\
&\leqslant K_{0}\bigl(Cu+2S_{n}(\mathcal{E})\bigr)S_{n}(\mathcal{E})\end{split} $$

for all $u\leqslant\tilde{r}/3$ .

Next, define

$$ c(x;e,\tilde{e},\eta,\hat{\eta})=\bigl[f(e(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))\bigr]-\bigl[f(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))\bigr] $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ so that

$$ \bigl(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e)\bigr)-\bigl(\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-M_{n}(\tilde{e})\bigr)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(X_{i};e,\tilde{e},\eta,\hat{\eta}). $$

Fix $k,\ell\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ . By Taylor’s theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder,

$$ \displaystyle|c(X_{i};e,\tilde{e},\eta,\hat{\eta})| \displaystyle=|[f(e(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))]-[f(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))-f(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))]| \displaystyle=|f_{w}(e(X_{i}),\eta_{1}(X_{i}))^{\top}(\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i}))-f_{w}(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta_{2}(X_{i}))^{\top}(\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i}))| \displaystyle\leqslant\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}\|f_{w}(e(X_{i}),\eta_{1}(X_{i}))-f_{w}(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))\|_{2} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}\|f_{w}(e(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))-f_{w}(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))\|_{2} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}\|f_{w}(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta(X_{i}))-f_{w}(\tilde{e}(X_{i}),\eta_{2}(X_{i}))\|_{2} \displaystyle\leqslant 2C\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}^{2}+C\|\hat{\eta}(X_{i})-\eta(X_{i})\|_{2}|\tilde{e}(X_{i})-e(X_{i})|. $$

We have omitted subscripts $k\ell$ on $c$ and $f$ everywhere in the preceding display for brevity (i.e., $c$ above denotes $c_{k\ell}$ and $f$ above denotes $f_{k\ell}$ ). The functions $e_{1}(x)$ and $e_{2}(x)$ are somewhere on the line segment between $e(x)$ and $\tilde{e}(x)$ , and he functions $\eta_{1}(x)$ and $\eta_{2}(x)$ are somewhere on the line segment between $\eta(x)$ and $\hat{\eta}(x)$ , and the final inequality follows from uniform boundedness of $f_{ww}$ and $f_{w}^{\prime}$ . We conclude

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u}\|(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e))-(\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-M_{n}(\tilde{e}))\| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|c(X_{i};e,\tilde{e},\eta,\hat{\eta})\| \displaystyle\leqslant Cp^{2}\bigl(2\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}+u\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}\bigr) $$

where the last inequality follows by Cauchy-Schwarz. Recalling $\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e}))\preccurlyeq\tilde{K}I$ whenever $B_{n}$ holds, we conclude

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant u}\nabla\Psi(R_{n}(\tilde{e}))^{\top}[(\hat{M}_{n}(e)-M_{n}(e))-(\hat{M}_{n}(\tilde{e})-M_{n}(\tilde{e}))]\bm{1}(B_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\tilde{K}Cp^{2}(2\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}+u\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}) $$

for all $u\leqslant r/3$ . The preceding display and (101) imply Lemma C.4 in view of the decomposition (100). ∎

Continuing with the proof of Step 4, let $C_{n}=A_{n}\cap B_{n}$ and $r=r_{0}\wedge\beta>0$ , where $A_{n}$ and $r_{0}$ are as in (76) with $\hat{e}=\tilde{e}$ and $B_{n}$ and $\beta$ are as in (99). Fix $M>-\infty$ and an arbitrary sequence $a_{n}\uparrow\infty$ . For each $j>M$ with $2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\leqslant r$ , define the “shell” $S_{j}=\{e\in\mathcal{F}_{n}:2^{j-1}a_{n}\alpha_{n}<\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant 2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\}$ . It follows that for each such $j$ , whenever $e\in S_{j}$ we have $r_{0}\geqslant r\geqslant\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\geqslant 2^{j-1}a_{n}\alpha_{n}$ , and so by (76), we have

$$ (\phi_{n}(e)-\phi_{n}(\tilde{e}))\bm{1}(C_{n})\leqslant-c_{0}\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}\bm{1}(C_{n})\leqslant-c_{0}2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\bm{1}(C_{n}) $$

for all $e\in S_{j}$ . Hence using the definition of $\hat{e}$

$$ \displaystyle\bm{1}(\hat{e}\in S_{j})\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\bm{1}\biggl(\,\sup_{e\in S_{j}}\hat{\phi}_{n}(e)-\hat{\phi}_{n}(\tilde{e})\geqslant 0\biggr)\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\bm{1}\biggl(\,\sup_{e:\|e-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant 2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}}(\hat{\phi}_{n}(e)-\hat{\phi}_{n}(\tilde{e}))-(\phi_{n}(e)-\phi_{n}(\tilde{e}))\geqslant c_{0}2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\biggr)\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\bm{1}\bigl(2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}\geqslant c_{0}C_{0}^{-1}2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\bigr)\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}}{c_{0}C_{0}^{-1}2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}}\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{C_{0}}{c_{0}}\biggl(\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}}{2^{j-2}a_{n}\alpha_{n}}+\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}}{2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}}\biggr)\bm{1}(C_{n}) $$

where the last inequality follows from Lemma C.4. Then

$$ \displaystyle\bm{1}\left(\frac{r}{2}\geqslant\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}>2^{M}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\right)\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{j>M,2^{j}a_{n}\alpha_{n}\leqslant r}\bm{1}(\hat{e}\in S_{j})\bm{1}(C_{n}) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C_{0}}{c_{0}}\sum_{j=M+1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}}{2^{j-2}a_{n}\alpha_{n}}+\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}}{2^{2j-2}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{C_{0}}{c_{0}}\left(\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}}{2^{M-2}a_{n}\alpha_{n}}+\frac{4}{3}\frac{\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}}{2^{2M}a_{n}^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}}\right). $$

Since $\|\hat{\eta}-\eta\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(a_{n}\alpha_{n})$ , we conclude

$$ \textnormal{Pr}(r/2\geqslant\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}>2^{M}a_{n}\alpha_{n},C_{n})=o(1) $$

for each $M$ . Now, by step 3 we know that $\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}=o_{p}(1)$ . Applying step 3 again but with $\hat{\eta}=\eta$ shows $\|\tilde{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})=o_{p}(1)$ . Thus

$$ \|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|e^{*}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}=o_{p}(1) $$

so that $\textnormal{Pr}(\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}>r/2)=o(1)$ . Since $\textnormal{Pr}(C_{n})\rightarrow 1$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ , we can conclude that

$$ \textnormal{Pr}(\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}>2^{M}a_{n}\alpha_{n})=o(1). $$

With $a_{n}\uparrow\infty$ arbitrary, by the preceding display and Lemma B.2 we have $\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(\alpha_{n})$ and

$$ \|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}\leqslant\|\hat{e}-\tilde{e}\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|\tilde{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}) $$

as desired.

It remains to show the same convergence rate holds out of sample, i.e., $\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n})$ . We do this by showing that $\big|\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}-\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\big|=O_{p}(n^{-1/4})$ . With $\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-}$ as defined in Lemma B.5 in terms of the collection $\mathcal{E}$ of Assumption 5.1, we know that

$$ \displaystyle\big|\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}^{2}-\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}^{2}\big| \displaystyle=\Big|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[(\hat{e}(X_{i})-e^{*}(X_{i}))^{2}-\int_{\mathcal{X}}(\hat{e}(x)-e^{*}(x))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}P(x)]\Big| \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-}}|(P_{n}-P)e|. $$

Furthermore, by Lemma B.3 and Lemma B.5 we know that for some $K_{0}<\infty$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-}}|(P_{n}-P)f| \displaystyle\leqslant K_{0}n^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon \displaystyle\leqslant K_{0}\sqrt{2}n^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\epsilon/4,\mathcal{E},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}\epsilon \displaystyle=4K_{0}\sqrt{2}n^{-1/2}\int_{0}^{1/4}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{E},L^{2}(P_{n}))}\,\mathrm{d}\delta. $$

Then by (30) we conclude $\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{2}^{-}}|(P_{n}-P)e|=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ . Since

$$ |a-b|\leqslant a+b\implies\sqrt{|a-b|}\leqslant\sqrt{a+b}\implies|a-b|\leqslant\sqrt{a+b}\sqrt{|a-b|}=\sqrt{|a^{2}-b^{2}|} $$

for any $a,b\geqslant 0$ , we have

$$ \big|\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}-\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}\big|=O_{p}(n^{-1/4}) $$

as desired. ∎

### C.10 Proof of Theorem 5.1

Here we prove convergence of Algorithm 1, our concave maximization procedure for designing an optimal CSBAE. We begin by proving we can design for $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ , as stated in the first numbered condition of Theorem 5.1. The proof proceeds by showing that the objective defining $e_{t,\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*}(\cdot)$ in (35) can be written in a form so that Assumption 5.1 and (34) are satisfied, the latter with $\alpha_{N}=N^{-1/4}$ . Then we conclude by applying Lemma 5.2.

Many of our expressions will include the cumulative sum of batch frequencies $\sum_{u=1}^{t}\kappa_{u}$ . We use $\kappa_{1:t}$ to denote this quantity below. We similarly abbreviate $\sum_{u=1}^{t}N_{u}$ to $N_{1:t}$ .

With $V_{0:t,\textnormal{AIPW}}$ scalar, the information function $\Psi=\Psi(\cdot)$ is simply an increasing scalar-valued function by Assumption 5.2, and hence we have

$$ \displaystyle e_{t,\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*}(\cdot)=\argmax_{e_{t}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{*,t}}(V_{0:t,\textnormal{AIPW}})^{-1} \displaystyle=\argmin_{e_{t}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{*,t}}V_{0:t,\textnormal{AIPW}} \displaystyle=\argmax_{e_{t}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{*,t}}h(V_{0:t,\textnormal{AIPW}}) \displaystyle=\argmax_{e_{t}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{F}_{t,*}}\mathbb{E}_{P^{X}}\left[\frac{2C}{\gamma_{0}}-\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e_{0}^{(t)}(X)}-\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e_{0}^{(t)}(X)}\right] $$

where in the final equality we dropped the additive term $\mathbb{E}[(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{2}]$ which is independent of $e_{t}(\cdot)$ , and defined $h(x)=2C/\gamma_{0}-x$ for

$$ \gamma_{0}:=\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{2}\frac{1}{\kappa_{1:t}}\min(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{t})>0. $$

Evidently $h(\cdot)$ is decreasing. We can now define the information matrix

$$ \mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}(e_{t},\eta_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{P^{X}}\left[\frac{2C}{\gamma_{0}}-\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e_{0}^{(t)}(X)}-\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e_{0}^{(t)}(X)}\right] $$

which is of the form (28) with

$$ f(e,w)=\frac{2C}{\gamma_{0}}-\frac{w_{1}}{1-w_{3}-w_{4}e}-\frac{w_{2}}{w_{3}+w_{4}e} $$

and

$$ \eta(x)=\biggl(v_{0}(0,x),\,v_{0}(1,x),\,\frac{1}{\kappa_{1:t}}\sum_{u=1}^{t-1}\kappa_{u}e_{u}(x),\,\frac{1}{\kappa_{1:t}}\kappa_{t}\biggr). $$

Let $\mathcal{W}=[c,C]^{2}\times\mathcal{W}_{+}$ where $\mathcal{W}_{+}=\{(x,y)\in\real^{2}\mid x\geqslant\gamma_{0},y\geqslant\gamma_{0},x+y\leqslant 1-\gamma_{0}\}$ . By (3) and the assumptions of the Theorem (specifically the uniform bounds on the variance functions and the assumption that $\epsilon_{1}\leqslant e_{1}(x)=\hat{e}_{1}^{(k)}(x)\leqslant 1-\epsilon_{1}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ ), we can verify that $\eta(x)\in\mathcal{W}$ and $\hat{\eta}^{(k)}(x)\in\mathcal{W}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ , and sufficiently large $N$ , where

$$ \hat{\eta}^{(k)}(x)=\biggl(\hat{v}^{(k)}(0,x),\,\hat{v}^{(k)}(1,x),\,\frac{1}{N_{1:t}}\sum_{u=1}^{t-1}N_{u}\hat{e}_{u}^{(k)}(x),\,\frac{N_{t}}{N_{1:t}}\biggr). $$

Also we have

$$ 1-\gamma_{0}\geqslant w_{3}+w_{4}e\geqslant\gamma_{0}\quad\text{and}\quad f(e,w)\geqslant 0,\quad\forall(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}. $$

Evidently $\mathcal{W}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. With $w_{3}+w_{4}e$ linear in $e$ , there exists $\delta<0$ such that for all $(e,w)$ in a neighborhood containing $(\delta,1-\delta)\times\mathcal{W}$ , $w_{3}+w_{4}e$ is uniformly bounded away from 0 and then $f(e,w)$ evidently has continuous second partial derivatives on this neighborhood. Finally, we compute

$$ -f^{\prime\prime}(e,w)=\frac{2w_{2}w_{4}^{2}}{(w_{3}+w_{4}e)^{3}}+\frac{2w_{1}w_{4}^{2}}{(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)^{3}}\geqslant\frac{2c\gamma_{0}^{2}}{(1-\gamma_{0})^{3}}>0,\quad\forall(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W} $$

which shows that all conditions of Assumption 5.1 have been satisfied. Equation (34) holds with $\alpha_{N}=N^{-1/4}$ by (46) and (17), completing the proof of the first numbered condition of Theorem 5.1, pertaining to design for $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ .

It remains to show the second numbered condition holds. As above, the proof proceeds by showing the objective for $\hat{e}_{t,\textnormal{EPL}}^{*}(\cdot)$ in (35) can be written in a form so that Assumption 5.1 and (34) are satisfied, the latter with $\alpha_{N}=N^{-1/4}$ . To that end, we take $\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}(e_{t},\eta_{0})=V_{0:t,\textnormal{EPL}}^{-1}$ which takes the form (28) with

$$ f(e,w)=f(e,w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4},w_{5})=\frac{(w_{3}+w_{4}e)(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}{w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}w_{5}w_{5}^{\top} $$

and

$$ \eta(x)=\biggl(v_{0}(0,x),\,v_{0}(1,x),\,\frac{1}{\kappa_{1:t}}\sum_{u=1}^{t-1}\kappa_{u}e_{u}(x),\,\frac{\kappa_{t}}{\kappa_{1:t}},\,\psi(x)\biggr). $$

Let $\mathcal{W}=[c,C]^{2}\times\mathcal{W}_{+}\times[-C,C]^{p}\subseteq\real^{4+p}$ , where once again $\mathcal{W}_{+}=\{(x,y)\in\real^{2}\mid x\geqslant\gamma_{0},y\geqslant\gamma_{0},x+y\leqslant 1-\gamma_{0}\}$ for

$$ \gamma_{0}:=\frac{\epsilon_{1}}{2\kappa_{1:t}}\min(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{t})>0. $$

Evidently $\mathcal{W}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. Then the assumptions of the Theorem (specifically the uniform bounds on the variance functions and the assumption that $\epsilon_{1}\leqslant e_{1}(x)=\hat{e}_{1}^{(k)}(x)\leqslant 1-\epsilon_{1}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ ) ensure that for each fold $k=1,\ldots,K$ , if we take

$$ \hat{\eta}^{(k)}(x)=\biggl(\hat{v}^{(k)}(0,x),\,\hat{v}^{(k)}(1,x),\,\frac{1}{N_{1:t}}\sum_{u=1}^{t-1}N_{u}\hat{e}_{u}^{(k)}(x),\,\frac{N_{t}}{N_{1:t}},\,\psi(x)\biggr) $$

then $\eta(x)\in\mathcal{W}$ and $\hat{\eta}^{(k)}(x)\in\mathcal{W}$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ whenever $N$ is sufficiently large. We note that for each $e\in[0,1]$ ,

$$ f(e,w)=\frac{(w_{3}+w_{4}e)(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}{w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}w_{5}w_{5}^{\top} $$

is positive semidefinite because the lead constant above is nonnegative. Furthermore, note that the denominator $w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)$ is bounded below by $c$ for any $(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}$ and continuous on $(e,w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4})\in\real^{5}$ . This denominator is linear in $e$ (for fixed $w$ ) and so additionally there exists $\delta<0$ such that on some open neighborhood containing $(\delta,1-\delta)\times\mathcal{W}$ , this denominator is strictly positive. Therefore $f(e,w)$ has two continuous partial derivatives with respect to $e$ . Finally, we compute

$$ -f^{\prime\prime}(e,w)=\frac{2w_{4}^{2}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}{(w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e))^{3}}w_{5}w_{5}^{\top}. $$

This is positive semidefinite since as above, $1-\gamma_{0}\geqslant w_{3}+w_{4}e\geqslant\gamma_{0}$ for all $(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}$ , so

$$ \frac{2w_{4}^{2}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}{(w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e))^{3}}>0 $$

on $[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}$ . Furthermore, as all diagonal entries of $w_{5}w_{5}^{\top}$ are nonnegative, the inclusion of an intercept in $\psi(x)$ ensures that

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}}\textnormal{tr}(-f^{\prime\prime}(e,w)) \displaystyle\geqslant\inf_{(e,w)\in[0,1]\times\mathcal{W}}\,\frac{2w_{4}^{2}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)}{[w_{1}(w_{3}+w_{4}e)+w_{2}(1-w_{3}-w_{4}e)]^{3}} \displaystyle\geqslant\frac{2\gamma_{0}^{3}(1-\gamma_{0})}{C^{3}}. $$

As before, equation (34) holds with $\alpha_{N}=N^{-1/4}$ by (46) and (17), enabling us to apply Lemma 5.2 and completing the proof of the Theorem.

### D.2 Perfect nuisance estimation

To better isolate the performance effects of our specific choices of nuisance estimation methods in the numerical study of Section 6, in Tables 5 and 6 we reproduce Tables 1 and 2, respectively, but assume all nuisance functions are known exactly at both the design and estimation stages. For ATE estimation (Table 5), the flexible designs are aware of a perfectly constant variance function in the homoskedastic DGPs, which induces them to always learn the (optimal) simple RCT in every simulation. However, for the binned designs in the homoskedastic DGPs and both the binned and flexible designs in the heteroskedastic DGPs, there is some cross-simulation variability in the propensity learned. This stems from variation in the parts of the variance function being sampled due to variation in the covariates across simulations. Consequently, the simulated finite sample efficiency gain ends up being somewhat lower than the asymptotic gain. This suggests that the finite sample efficiency gains from pooling observed in Table 1 are due to improved use of nuisance function estimates by the pooled estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ . One reason we might expect this is that the pooled estimator uses nuisance estimates from observations pooled across both batches of the experiment, while each component of the linearly aggregated estimator only uses nuisance estimates from a single batch.

In Table 6, however, we still see some finite sample efficiency gains from pooling, though the effect is not as large as in Table 2 in the main text. We attribute this to the fact that for estimating $\theta_{0,\textnormal{PL}}$ , pooling allows the asymptotic variance to be approached more quickly as a function of the total sample size $N$ . Such an effect does not show up in ATE estimation with AIPW, since for $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*}$ and $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*}$ the oracle estimators of Section 3, we can see that $N\textnormal{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*})=V_{0,\textnormal{AIPW}}$ exactly for all $N$ while $N\textnormal{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*})$ only approaches $V_{0,\textnormal{EPL}}$ asymptotically as $N\rightarrow\infty$ . So letting $A_{N}^{*}$ be the (finite sample) AMSE of $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*}$ computed on a sample of size $N$ , we’d expect $NA_{N}^{*}>2NA_{2N}^{*}$ . Then averaging two independent copies of $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*}$ on $N$ observations yields an estimator with AMSE $A_{N}^{*}/2$ , while pooling would yield an estimator with AMSE $A_{2N^{*}}$ .
